newsitem.title: FRANCE: French deputies slam Britain over mad cow crisis.
newsitem.headline: French deputies slam Britain over mad cow crisis.

text.p: A French parliamentary commission on Tuesday blasted Britain for hiding the full facts about mad cow disease and accused London of trying to blackmail its neighbours in the 10-month-old beef crisis.

A six-month inquiry set up by the National Assembly (lower house) found "intolerable" lapses in Britain's handling of the affair, inadequate controls by the European Union and a lack of coordination in France, a report issued on Tuesday showed.

The report's author, French deputy Jean-Francois Mattei, said there was no question of quickly lifting the embargo on British beef, imposed after the crisis over mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), erupted last March.
"French politicians are not ready to accept an end to the embargo on British meat," he told a news conference on the report's findings. "This situation is a necessary one," he said.

The 200-page document, together with nearly 700 pages of evidence given to a special parliamentary committee, is the most detailed French investigation yet into the disease, which has been killing British herds and alarming shoppers across Europe.
Reviving a row over Britain's "non-cooperation" tactics in trying to get the ban lifted, the report said London had failed to show cooperation or a sense of its partners' interests.
"It is unacceptable that political blackmail can be used by one member to block collective decisions taken in a community linked together by solidarity," it said.
Britain adopted a policy of non-cooperation, blocking some EU business, for several weeks before EU leaders agreed a compromise on lifting the ban at a Florence summit last June.
So far the European Union says conditions agreed then for a gradual lifting of the global export ban have not been met.

The French report also heaped blame on Britain for failing to pass on all the results of its research into mad cow disease, although it also said the progress of British research may have discouraged French scientists from speeding up their own work.

Scientists are looking for proof of a suspected link between BSE and a fatal human brain disorder, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). They are also studying whether -- as many suspect -- BSE spreads through herds in feed containing bonemeal and offal.
A British farm ministry spokeswoman said all public research was available to anyone who needed it.
The report reflected French anger over what it called an "intolerable" decision by Britain to allow the export of feed containing bone extracts after banning its use at home in 1988.
Britain says it did not immediately ban bonemeal exports because it was still legal to feed it to pigs and poultry, despite the domestic ban on giving it to cattle, sheep or goats.
France banned imports of the British bonemeal in 1990.
To get round the restrictions, feed producers may have used Belgium as a "laundering" shop to allow suspect British feed to be relaballed and then passed off as Irish, the report said.
Customs figures show bonemeal imports to France from Belgium or Luxembourg jumped from 1,842 tonnes in 1987 to 3,566 tonnes in 1988. By 1995, the figure had shot up to 18,292 tonnes.
"With this in mind, we cannot avoid the hypothesis that this country (Belgium) might have welcomed in British feed which was trying to lose its identity," the French report said.
Earlier this month Mattei denied a French newspaper report that Belgium would be criticised in the parliament's findings.
